conflict.would_settle: Two things, in order. (1) An owner ruling on what the darg1241 record represents: Glottolog's 'North-Central Dargwa' [dar] contains as dialects Megeb/Mehweb [mege1234] (fixed second syllable: Moroz 2019, 2015, two first-hand works), Aqusha-Uraxi [aqus1234] = the literary base (no clearly expressed stress, weak final: Musaev 1999 first-hand; vs 'fixed, most often initial': Borise 2018 carrying Abdullaev 1954: 62; vs 'northern lects fixed second syllable': Moroz 2015 carrying Abdullaev 1954: 23-71) and Cudaxar/Gapshin-Butrin [cuda1238, gaps1234] = the Tsudaqar group (free, phonemic, numerous minimal pairs: Borise 2018 carrying Abdullaev 1954, Moroz 2014, Shakhbanova 2007; 'salient dynamic stress': Musaev 1999). If the record is split per dialect, Mehweb resolves to FIXED second (rule 01 010 0100..., listed exceptions) on the read record and Tsudaqar to lexical on carried evidence only. (2) For the literary/Akusha leg, which stays disputed even after a split (primary 'no clear stress, weak final' vs carried 'fixed mostly initial' vs carried 'second syllable'), the original pages of Abdullaev, S.N. 1954, Grammatika darginskogo jazyka, pp. 6-11, 23-71, 62 (bibliography row 9, scan-and-deliver: Widener offsite 1274.260.20), or van den Berg 2001, Dargi folktales... introduction to Dargi grammar (row 3, HathiTrust search-only; Widener PK9201.D38 B47 2001), or Abdullaev et al. 2014 Sovremennyj darginskij jazyk (row 5, print-only), or the unopenable Moroz 2014 cross-dialect survey (row 6, academia.edu behind Cloudflare) would settle initial vs second vs weak-final for Akusha.

1042.cfw: Moroz 2019 and Moroz 2015 give Mehweb fixed second-syllable stress, Musaev 1999 and Borise 2018 (after Abdullaev 1954) give the Tsudaqar dialects free contrastive stress, and Moroz 2015 adds that other Dargwa lects stress various syllables, so all sources agree the varieties differ and the only open point is whether literary Akusha Dargwa has weak initial stress (Borise 2018 after Abdullaev 1954) or no clear word stress at all (Musaev 1999).

tn.translation: Thus, in Dâw there are two types of tones, which are always contour tones: rising tone /V́/ and falling tone /V̀/, and there are toneless words (zero tone ∅). ... In tonal monomorphemic words only one tone occurs, which falls on the stressed syllable, which is obligatorily the last syllable of the word ... 1049.prule: No stress rule. 1051.dq: Word stress is predictable in CDA, and follows a number of rules that are common amongst other conservative Arabic dialects, as in MSA.

1051.heavy: Three-way scale: superheavy CvCC and Cv̄C (word-final, stressed if present); heavy Cv̄ and CvC (rightmost non-final one stressed); light Cv. Rhodokanakis 1911: 'Langvokal und geminierter Radikal' hold the stress.
1051.dflt: leftmost light syllable Cv, i.e. initial (wáraqa, šárika — examples only up to three syllables); but CvCvC verb stems and disyllabic nouns stress the final CvC (waṣál, ktúb, qmár)
1051.prule: Word stress predictable by syllable weight (Davey 2013 §2.9): (a) a final superheavy syllable CvCC or Cv̄C is stressed if present (māṣū́r, halūmā́t, ġallḗt); (b) otherwise the rightmost non-final heavy syllable Cv̄ or CvC (xā́tim, mubánnad, múrtafaʕ); (c) otherwise the leftmost light syllable (wáraqa, šárika); (d) basic verb stems CvCvC are iambic, stress on the final CvC (ktúb, fṭán, waṣál), and disyllabic CvCv́C nouns likewise (qamar > qmár 'first vowel unstressed').
1051.srule: Not mentioned in Davey 2013 section 2.9 (p. 68; primary-stress rules only). 1054.prule: Stress is weak ('not sharply expressed, hard to catch'), not fixed to any syllable, and 'fully dependent on vowel length': (4) a word with one long vowel is stressed on it; (6) with several long and short vowels stress gravitates to the long vowel nearest the end; (5) all-long words are stressed on the last syllable; (1) all-short disyllabic nouns always final, (2) all-short tri-/polysyllables usually final, but (3) all-short trisyllables ending in weak -æ take the second syllable; (7) long+short disyllables ending in -й often final. General drift: 'stress always strives toward the end of the word'. Position of a short vowel before a consonant cluster also 'plays an important role' (not elaborated). Plural formation moves stress (æрфуг -> ǽрфгутæ initial; 3-syllable all-short plurals penultimate); loans keep source stress; attribute+noun, noun+postposition, compound verbs and clitics form accentual complexes with one stress.

1055.prule: Expiratory stress (Starkton) with a strong initial-syllable tendency: nouns of 3+ syllables stress the first syllable when the final syllable is open; a closed (heavy, 'halblang') final syllable draws a secondary and possibly the main accent (first syllable keeps high pitch); disyllables with open final = initial Starkton, disyllables with closed final = no marked Starkton / final may sound accented; all plurals and suffixed (ablative) forms = initial Starkton regardless of length; verbs = Starkton on the root (= first) syllable regardless of length (§84d, §320).
1055.srule: Kauczor marks a Nebenakzent (`) distinct from the Starkton: in non-compound nouns of three or more syllables with a closed final syllable, that final syllable carries a Nebenakzent, which may be strengthened to the main accent, the first syllable keeping high pitch (dèdigár, §74); before the copula -n, polysyllabic nouns take a Nebenakzent on the last syllable (ondì-n, §77c); in verbs a Nebenakzent sits on the vowel that takes the shifted accent, shown only in the paradigms (§320). Plurals and suffixed nouns: first syllable only, whatever the length. No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described.

1056.prule: Two-tone system (H, L) with the vowel as TBU; all combinations of H and L occur on mono- and disyllabic words (HH, HL, LH, LL, plus contour patterns on long vowels); tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive (e.g. interrogative formed by imposing H on the imperative). 1061.prule: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (quantity-insensitive); secondary stresses on the first syllable of each following 'stress group' (1-3 syllables), where stress-group boundaries are set segmentally (consonant clusters, [+distributed] onsets), not by syllable count.
1061.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of each non-initial stress group. Words divide into one to four stress groups of one to three syllables, bounded segmentally (inside consonant clusters and before laminal/[+distributed] consonants; disyllabic preferred), each with one stress on its first syllable; a monosyllabic open (CV) group is never stressed, and /a/ can pull a secondary stress one syllable rightward. Positions therefore depend on the segments, not on syllable count.

tn.quote: It is necessary to specify here the phonetic characteristics of stress in Djinang. Three parameters are involved; namely, pitch, duration and fortis articulation (Hyman, 1975:207). Primary stress has the highest pitch, and since primary stress normally occurs word initially, most Djinang words commence with higher pitch which falls slowly as the word is articulated, with a sharp drop in pitch on the last syllable. If the primary stress occurs on the second syllable, pitch rises to a maximum in the nucleus of the primary-stressed syllable, and falls thereafter.

1062.dq: In Dobel the phonological word is defined as a stress group. Each phonological word is the domain of one primary stress which occurs on the nuclear syllable of the phonological word.
1062.dloc: Section 4 'The Phonological Word', journal pp. 60-61 (rules (1)-(2) and Observations 1)-2)); Appendix A 'Stress in the orthography', pp. 65-66; Footnote on the one exception /ta'matu/ (Footnotes, c. p. 75).
1062.prule: Lexical (contrastive) stress inside a right-edge window of the grammatical ROOT: primary stress falls unpredictably on either the penultimate (more common) or the final syllable of the root; a root-final voiceless-plosive+/u/ syllable (/ʔu/, /tu/) is extrametrical, so such roots surface with antepenultimate stress (one exception, /ta'matu/). Stress never falls on affixes or clitics and affixation does not shift it. Minimal pairs exist (/'tamin/ vs /ta'nin/; /'tayi/ vs /ta+'yi/).

The primary source (Hughes & Hughes 1989, Section 4) and Hughes 1995 mark one primary stress per phonological word and do not mention secondary stress.

1063.dq: 5.1 The phonological word in Dobu is usually of from one to 10 syllables, with one primary stress and regularly patterned secondary stresses, bounded by juncture. (See 5.2)
1063.prule: Stress non-phonemic (predictable, not contrastive). Disyllables: penultimate (initial). Trisyllables: 'in many' antepenultimate, but examples show both penult (e'ta.i, e'ta.la, gi'da.ba, tʰe'tʰela) and antepenult ('ma.i.na, 'bagula), and some fluctuate ('tʰamagu ~ tʰa'magu). Words of 4+ syllables parsed as concatenations of 2- or 3-syllable stress groups (2+2, 3+2, 2+3, 2+2+3...), each group carrying its own stress; the parse is listed per word, not derived by rule. No weight conditioning (all syllables open, length non-phonemic).
1063.srule: Stated: each phonological word has 'one primary stress and regularly patterned secondary stresses' (5.1); words of 4+ syllables are combinations of 2- or 3-syllable stress groups (2+2, 3+2, 2+3, 2+2+3..., listed per word up to 14 syllables), each group stressed like a 2-/3-syllable word ('wa.i 'wa.i, 'e.si'nu.a, 'i.la.i 'la.ma, 'a.i 'a.i.la, ʔi'mwa.la 'to.ni), so non-primary stresses fall on every second or third syllable; the 2-vs-3 grouping is not predictable and the lists use one stress mark throughout, so which group stress is the primary is not stated.

1064.tone: Tida explicitly rejects both 'stress accent' and 'pitch accent' labels for Dom: the contrast is in melody shape (H / HL / LH per word), not accent location ('it is not an issue where the accent is, but what the pattern is'). Clitics lose their own tone and take a 'clitic-type' low tone; verbs change tone class under inflection (§2.4.7.2, Table 2.5). 1066.prule: Two-tone system (level 55 vs falling 53) on full syllables plus a toneless/neutral-tone (31) reduced syllable type. Stress follows syllable type, not position: full-tone (root/main) syllables are stressed, reduced neutral-tone syllables (presyllables, affixes, particles) are unstressed. Disyllables are typically iambic (reduced presyllable + stressed main syllable, ~87% of disyllabic words); root+suffix disyllables are trochaic.
1066.srule: No secondary stress ranked below a primary is described: stress goes with syllable type (full tonal syllables stressed, reduced neutral-tone syllables unstressed), so trisyllabic words have one unstressed syllable, first or second, 'with the other two syllables getting nearly equal stress' (tə³¹lɑm⁵³bɔŋ⁵³ 'egret'), and fixed four-syllable phrases and compounds reduce syllables 1 and 3, leaving 2 and 4 stressed.
1066.quote: In disyllabic words, which make up most of the lexicon, Trung is a strongly sesquisyllabic (“one-and-a-half syllable”) language, featuring an unstressed presyllable followed by a stressed main syllable. This “iambic” pattern is very much in keeping with other Tibeto-Burman languages and languages of Southeast Asia. ... One statistical analysis of a small Trung lexicon (Dai and Liu 1987) found that some 87% of all disyllabic words have a reduced first syllable. ... Compounds with three syllables ... may have a reduced syllable in any position, depending on the compound’s constituent parts ... …
1066.loc: Perlin 2019 ch. 2 'Stress and Rhythm' pp. 59-61 and 'Tone' pp. 61-62; ch. 3 'Phonological and Morphological Word in Trung' p. 70. LaPolla 2017 draft section 2 (Phonology), p. 2 of PDF.
1066.idn: Perlin: 'Trung', primarily the Third Township variety (Dulong River valley); LaPolla: 'Dulong', First Township dialect spoken in Dizhengdang (a named variety of the language); data: Perlin: Dúlóng River Valley (Gongshan, Yunnan), documentation project begun 2009, intensive fieldwork into 2011, follow-up trips 2014…
1066.exq_: Grammatical particles and affixes are generally unstressed, resulting in a disyllabic word with stress on the initial syllable and a less typical trochaic pattern, e.g. ɛt⁵⁵ɕɯ³¹ ‘laugh’. (Also: 'some 87% of all disyllabic words have a reduced first syllable.')
1066.tone: Perlin: syllable is the TBU, tone lexically specified on every root; two contrastive tones (level 55, falling 53) plus 'neutral tone'/toneless 31 on reduced syllables (affixes, particles, presyllable of most disyllables); checked syllables carry one short high tone; low functional load (minimal pairs ~3% of lexicon, Liu 1989) and much apparent free variation between 55 and 53. LaPolla 2017 concurs: 'one of two tones, level... or falling..., but the structure of many words is sesquisyllabic, where the first part of the word is an unstressed, toneless, CV syllable' making 'something like a three-tone contrast'; no tone sandhi but grammatical falling->level alternation. Stress is described only as the correlate of full vs reduced (toneless) syllables; no positional word-stress rule.

tn.translation: 4-1. Duala uses pitch opposition for distinctive purposes; in a CVCV sequence each syllable carries a tone; there are three relevant levels: high tone: ná 'that' ... mid tone: nā 'there it is' ... low tone: nà 'and, with' ... Modulated tones are also found; they come with a lengthening of the vowel that bears them ... complex tones will therefore be treated as a succession of two simple tones on a geminate vowel and written: ^ for the falling tone, ˇ for the rising tone, without doubling the vowel.
